item.title: W01 Instructor Framing — Woodland Gloss
item.description: Private instructor synthesis. Not published. Use to prep seminar voice, discussion pivots, and live examples.High Level: Manning & Massumi argued that "research-creation" is actually a way of refusing the institutional separation between thinking and making — treating the act of practice itself as the site where concepts are generated, not just applied.Dissertation Level: In my current work — whether it's the sonic sculpture series or the Somax2 sessions — this explains why I hit the impasse of feeling like the "intellectual" work (reading, writing the proposal) and the "technical" work (building the hardware/software system) were happening in separate rooms. I was assuming they were supposed to meet at the end (delivery of results) rather than interpenetrating the whole time. The dissertation chapters I've been struggling to write are stuck because I'm framing, not conditioning. I need to let the making speak, not just illustrate.Lab Level: Students need to care about this because their projects will be stale unless they stop treating the "concept part" and the "build part" as sequential phases. If you're doing your research first and then making the thing that illustrates it, you're not doing research-creation. The build IS the research. The question is how to make that visible in documentation. "What is your practice thinking right now? Not what are you making — what mode of thought is already active in the act of making it?" "Where in your current workflow do you experience the split between 'I'm working' and 'I'm thinking'? Can you locate the exact moment?" "Manning & Massumi say: 'unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects.' What in your practice functions as gravity — as the enabling resistance you need?" The Don't Play in My Hair sculpture is a useful live example of enabling constraints. The capacitive sensor grid on the hair sculpture doesn't interpret touch. It detects threshold crossings at electrode points. That reduction — from the full richness of touching someone's hair (texture, pressure, temperature, social charge) to a binary event at 12 points — is both a loss and a condition. The sculpture works because the machine can't feel what the touch means. The gap between what the sensor reads and what the human feels is the piece.This is what conditioning looks like: two co-causes (the sensor's reductive model, the culturally charged act of touching Black hair) brought into interaction. Neither cause alone produces the meaning. The interaction is the work.High Level: Agre argued that "critical technical practice" is actually a way of sustaining a split identity in research — one foot in building, one foot in critiquing — such that the work is always already reflecting on its own assumptions, not saving that reflection for a separate paper.Dissertation Level: In my work with Somax2 and sensor-based systems, this explains why I kept hitting the impasse of: "my technical experiments produce things, but I don't know how to write about them in a way that doesn't sound like either a user manual or a philosophical abstraction." That was the sign of the split identity not working. Agre's "intermediation" is the move I was missing — developing a vocabulary at the middle level of abstraction that bridges the phenomenological (what it feels like to play with Somax2) and the technical (what Somax2 actually does). The term I've been building toward — "transducing Black epistemologies" — is an intermediation term. It's neither fully technical nor fully philosophical.Lab Level: Students need to care about this because without the split identity, the Critical Technical Journal (ASN 2) becomes either a build log or a theory essay — and neither is what it's supposed to be. The journal works when the craft voice and the critique voice talk to each other in the same entry. You need both feet on the ground. "What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a crash, not a one-time failure — but something that happens again and again? That's your first hassle. Write it down." "Agre says his breakthrough was learning phenomenological philosophy 'on its own terms, not as a spec.' What would it mean to learn your current software stack on its terms — not what it can do for you, but what it's about?" "If your tools 'reinvent every site in their own image' — what image is your favorite tool reinventing the world as?" The OSC message schema I designed for the MPR121 sensors — /sensor/touch/[channel] — is an intermediation term. It's not called /capacitive_threshold_event (too technical) and it's not called /presence_of_hand (too phenomenological). "touch" is a middle-level abstraction that's legible to both the body and the system. Every time I name a data stream in OSC, I'm doing intermediation.The hassle I hit repeatedly: OSC over UDP drops packets when the Wi-Fi is contested. Latency spikes. The sensor responds, the software doesn't, and the interaction feels broken. This is a system hassle — a recurring friction that tells me something structural about the setup. The intermediation question: what's the right name for this impasse? Not "packet loss" (too technical) and not "the system feels dead" (too vague). Maybe: "the signal arrives but the presence doesn't."High Level: Magnusson argued that "epistemic tools" is actually a way of recognizing that when you pick up an instrument — any instrument — you're not just picking up a functional object but adopting a set of propositions about what the world is and what can be known about it.Dissertation Level: In my work, this explains the recurring tension between the Zoom H5 and my DAW. The H5 models my research sites as "mic placements in a room with specific gain staging." The DAW models them as "audio files at specific sample rates." Neither model is the sonic event I'm trying to capture — the presence of a space, the resonance of an object, the social charge of a material. The tool I'm using is always making a claim about what matters about sound. Part of the dissertation project is to make that claim explicit, contested, and productive — which means writing about the tools, not just with them.The Zoom as epistemic tool: it has an embodiment relation in the moment of recording (I act through it, attending to what the mic hears), but the files it produces immediately shift into a hermeneutic relation (I have to interpret what the recording means, what it captures and doesn't). Recognizing that shift is part of how I document practice.Lab Level: Students need to care about this because unless they can articulate what their tools claim about the world, they can't critique that claim — and their projects will just reproduce the assumptions of the default software without knowing it. "I used Ableton" is not a methodology statement. "Ableton models time as a horizontally-arranged grid of discrete regions, and I'm testing what happens when I treat that grid as a material resistance rather than a container" — that's a methodology statement. "Pick one button on your hardware or one default setting in your software. Who decided that was the default? Why?" "The MPR121 sees the world as 12 threshold events. What does it not see? What would need to change for it to see that?" "Magnusson says the digital system is 'material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control.' Which layer are you spending the most time in? Which are you ignoring?" In Sun Ra Cryosleep and Buffalo Soldier, the firmware on the microcontroller is doing the same basic work — reading sensor state, sending OSC messages — but the meaning of the touch events is entirely different. The circuits are the same; the epistemic framing is different. This is the clearest demo I can offer of Magnusson's point: the tool (the MPR121 + RP2040) is the same; but the instrument — the thing that makes meaning from the tool — is built by the design around it, the materials it touches, the cultural context it operates in.The hardware doesn't know it's touching Black hair. The intelligence is in the entanglement: sensor + material + audience + context + installation design. The epistemic tool is the whole configuration, not just the chip.Ask: "What are you complicit in right now? Not rhetorically — concretely. What system are you working inside of right now that you didn't choose?" Wait. Let it sit. Someone will say: Drexel. Someone will say: their laptop. Someone will say: Western music. All correct.Draw the split on the board. Put "writing the proposal" on one side and "building the thing" on the other. Ask: "Where does thinking happen?" Most point to the proposal side. Then: "But when you're building, what are you doing?" Let them find the word: thinking. Then erase the line.Return to the Woodland Gloss question: "What is this sensor claiming about the world?" Pull back to epistemics. The setup guide is for outside of class; the seminar is for this question."What's the electrode in your DAW? What's the thing that converts the world into your system's native representation? Start there." Manning & Massumi's enabling constraint ↔ Agre's hassle — both are framings of productive friction; one is generative, one is diagnostic. A hassle, worked carefully, can become an enabling constraint. Magnusson's black box ↔ Agre's computational imperialism — both describe what happens when a tool's assumptions become invisible and self-perpetuating. Manning & Massumi's conditioning ↔ Magnusson's amplification-reduction — conditioning is the practice; amplification-reduction is the mechanism. You condition by choosing which reductions are generative. Agre's split identity ↔ Manning & Massumi's prebifurcation point — the split identity is required precisely because institutions keep pulling the two feet apart. R-C is the attempt to stay at the prebifurcation point as long as possible.

item.title: Epistemic Tools Introduction
item.description:
"Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." — Hankins & Silverman, quoted in Magnusson If W01A established research-creation as the methodological orientation of this course, W01B establishes the epistemic status of the tools you work with. These two moves are connected: if making is already a mode of thinking, then the instrument you make with is already shaping the kinds of thought that are possible.This is what Magnusson, following Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, means by epistemic tools: instruments are not passive implements waiting to be used — they are active participants in the construction of knowledge. The choice of instrument is not neutral. It conditions what questions you can ask, what results you can produce, and — eventually — what you consider beautiful, interesting, or true.This puts tool choice in a new light. Choosing TouchDesigner over Processing, Max/MSP over SuperCollider, a capacitive sensor over a camera — these are not just technical decisions. They are epistemological ones.Don Ihde identified three phenomenological modalities of instrument-use — three ways that instruments mediate between the body and the world:You act through the instrument, which extends your body or amplifies your senses. The instrument recedes into the background — you experience through it, not at it. A well-practiced keyboard player doesn't think about the keys; they think about the music. The keys are an extension of the hand.The instrument produces data that you must interpret. A spectrograph, a heat map, an oscilloscope reading. The instrument mediates reality by translating it into a representation — but that representation requires interpretive work to become knowledge.The instrument becomes something you engage with for its own sake — as a quasi-other, a presence with its own agency. Virtual reality headsets, interactive installations, or a generative system that responds to you all produce this kind of relation. You are not acting through them; you are with them.Important: These modalities are not exclusive categories — they are tendencies. Any given practice involves mixtures and oscillations between them. And they are not value-neutral: each modality shapes what you notice, what you miss, and what you expect the instrument to do for you.Ihde's most directly practical insight: every instrument involves amplification-reduction transformations. It amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. There is no exception to this.A microphone amplifies pressure-wave events in a certain frequency range and reduces everything else. A MIDI controller amplifies discrete pitch/velocity events and reduces continuous, gestural sound. A capacitive touch sensor amplifies conductivity at specific points and reduces everything that isn't electrical contact.The danger is not that tools reduce — they have to. The danger is forgetting that they do. When the reduction becomes invisible, the thing not being captured disappears from your thinking entirely.Magnusson on software: Musical software encodes inherited defaults: equal-tempered tuning, temporal quantization, note-based event models. These are not facts about music — they are contingent historical choices that have been naturalized. They have become what Latour (and Bowker & Star) call black boxes.A black box is an object or system whose internal workings have become invisible through repeated use. Latour: objects "establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear."Bowker and Star extend this: "the more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory."Notice what this means for practice: the tools you're most fluent with are the most dangerous. Fluency produces blindness. The instrument you've used for years is the instrument whose assumptions you've most thoroughly absorbed into your practice without noticing.CTP connection (Agre): This is why the "split identity" matters — one foot in craft, one foot in critique. The craft foot needs fluency. The critique foot needs to keep opening the black boxes that fluency keeps closing.Agre's phrase names a specific version of this: computers "aim to reinvent virtually every other site of practice in its own image." They are built from representational models of the activities they will be used in. But they don't just represent — they restructure.A digital audio workstation doesn't just record and edit audio. It restructures the practice of making music around the concept of a timeline, discrete regions, channels, effects chains, automation curves. These aren't neutral containers — they are a model of music-making built by engineers with particular assumptions about what music is. "A computer, then, does not simply have an instrumental use in a given site of practice; the computer is frequently about that site in its very design." This is why Agre says that technical people often experience phenomenological texts as "sounding like mysticism." The mismatch isn't in the philosophy — it's that the computer's representational model and the phenomenologist's model of experience are genuinely incommensurable. You can't translate one into the other because they aren't the same kind of thing. Agre's solution: stop translating, start learning on their own terms.Magnusson frames the historical problem this way: Western philosophy has long separated techne (making, craft, technique) from episteme (knowledge, theory, science). Instruments of art were not instruments of knowledge; skill was not wisdom.This separation is now being productively challenged — by cognitive science (embodied cognition, enactivism), by STS (Science and Technology Studies), by research-creation methodology, and by practitioners in new interfaces for musical expression, interactive art, and critical making.The instruments become epistemic — fusing instrument with composition, as in the work of Gordon Mumma, David Tudor, or more recently in live-coding and instrument design. The digital system is, as Magnusson puts it, "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three registers are active at once.Three questions to hold as you work through this course:What does your tool amplify? What aspects of your practice does it make easier to see, hear, measure, or manipulate?What does your tool reduce? What is systematically missing from what your tool captures? What can't it represent — and how has that shaped what you've been making?Who designed the reduction? The defaults in your software were chosen by someone with specific assumptions. What were those assumptions, and whose experience of the world did they take as universal?These aren't rhetorical. They are the starting points for your Critical Technical Journal (ASN 2). Epistemic tool — an instrument that is a knowledge-making artifact; tools determine what is possible and thus what can be thought Embodiment / hermeneutic / alterity relations — Ihde's three phenomenological modalities of instrument-world relationship Amplification-reduction — every tool amplifies certain features and reduces others; no tool is neutral (Ihde) Black box — a naturalized object whose internal contingency has become invisible through repeated use (Latour, Bowker & Star) Computational imperialism — the tendency of computing to reinvent every site of practice in its own representational image (Agre) Techne / episteme — the historically-separated domains of craft-knowledge and theoretical-knowledge, now being rejoined Magnusson — Epistemic Tools4 (Ch. 3, selected sections)

The paradox at the heart of creative practice: the right constraint doesn't close things down — it opens them.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity is an implacable constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Add horizontal momentum, and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." Remove gravity and there's no arc — no lift, no landing, no jump as an event. The constraint is generative because of its resistance, not despite it.The enabling constraint is how this course thinks about everything from protocol choices to assignment structures. The MPR121 sensor's 12-point reduction is a constraint; it enables a certain kind of sculptural thinking. OSC over UDP dropping packets is a constraint; it forces a real-time compositional response to instability. The 3-hour seminar session is a constraint; it enables a depth of engagement that 50-minute sessions preclude.The critical move: distinguishing a constraint that merely limits from one that enables. Manning & Massumi: "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone." An enabling constraint is always a co-cause — it only becomes enabling in relation to something else it can push against.
Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 87 What in your practice functions as gravity — the implacable resistance you push against? Is it enabling or merely limitative? What would it take to make it enabling? What's the difference between a rule you've been given and a constraint you've designed? Have you ever designed a constraint for yourself that actually worked? When you hit a wall in a project, is it usually a limitative constraint (stop here) or an enabling one (find the co-cause)? How do you tell the difference in the moment? What would it mean to design the constraints of your project before you design its content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — Propositions 0–3; the concept of enabling constraints and conditioning is developed here in full.
Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Entanglement26   Failure as Method26   Physical-Digital Entanglement21Enabling ConstraintsPractitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.
Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality*3 — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Enabling Constraints20   Physical-Digital Entanglement21   Failure as Method26EntanglementFailure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.
Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice*5 — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.
Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Enabling Constraints20   Entanglement26   Collective Practice21Failure as MethodThe interweaving of physical materials, bodies, and environments with digital systems. Not an interface between two separate domains — an entanglement in which each shapes the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It is a series of transformations, each of which amplifies something and reduces something else. The body that touches the capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. What matters is knowing which something — and making that choice deliberately.Magnusson: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape how you hold it, where you put it, what it can touch. The firmware has temporal properties that shape the resolution and latency of the response. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across your hardware choices, your material selections, your installation environments, and your audience's bodies.
Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 103 At each arrow in your signal chain, what is being amplified and what is being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional — a design decision — or accidental? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing? And what creative or critical work can happen in that gap? Where in your practice does the physical environment shape the digital behavior — and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are you touching with your sensors or microcontrollers? What cultural, social, or political charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools*4 — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems and the phenomenology of digital tool relations.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality*3 — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects; the matter-network.
Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Enabling Constraints20   Entanglement26Physical-Digital EntanglementRendering work public is not the delivery of results. It is a continuation of the research — a way of making the formative conditions and processual transformation of the work available for encounter.Loveless, working through Haraway, argues that research-creation carries an obligation to render research public — not as a finished product submitted to evaluation, but as a practice in itself. What gets made public is not just the artifact but the forces that formed it: the impasses, the enabling constraints, the entanglements, the tools and their reductions. This is why the Final Presentation in this course is not a showcase. It is a rendering.The distinction Loveless makes is between transparency (showing your work) and accountability (taking responsibility for what your work does in the world — including what it can't do, what it excludes, and who it speaks to or past). Accountability requires knowing the stakes of the work, not just the process.For experimental media practice, making public also means confronting the question of audience: who is this for? What does it ask of the people who encounter it? A TouchDesigner patch sent to a hard drive is not public; the same patch running in a gallery space with bodies moving through it is. The difference is not technical. It is relational — and designing that relation is itself a creative and ethical act.
Week 67, Week 97, Week 114 What would it mean to make your process public — not just your result? What would you have to show that you've been hiding? Who is the audience for your work, and what does it ask of them? Have you designed that ask, or inherited it from the format? Loveless distinguishes transparency from accountability. Where in your practice are you being transparent (showing your method) without being accountable (owning what the work does or fails to do)? What form is your work made public in, and what does that form assume about who can access it?
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog*3 — on the obligation to render research public, curiosity as method, and the boundary object.
Research-Creation36   Collective Practice21   Failure as Method26   Entanglement26Making PublicThe studio is not a collection of individual practices happening in parallel. It is a site of collective becoming — where techniques of relation between practitioners are themselves a subject of inquiry.Manning & Massumi describe the seminar or studio event as a kind of experiment: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site." The condition: the potential for what might occur cannot be pre-reduced to "the delivery of already-arrived-at conclusions." This course is structured with that in mind. The critique, the potluck, the studio session — these are not performances of finished thinking. They are techniques of relation in the Manning & Massumi sense: devices for catalyzing interaction between practices at the level of their creative force.Critique, in this frame, is not judgment. It is activation — a practice of attending carefully to someone else's work in order to surface what it is doing that it may not know it's doing. A good critique question doesn't evaluate ("this works / this doesn't"). It opens ("what is this committed to? what does it refuse? what would it look like to follow that refusal further?").Collective practice also carries an ethic: you are responsible for what you bring to the room. Your presence, your attention, and your honest response to others' work are contributions to a shared intellectual environment. This is not a soft requirement. It is part of the assessment.
Week 29, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 114 What is the difference between a critique that evaluates and one that activates? What does an activating question sound like? What do you bring to the room as a practitioner that no one else does? What does the collective gain from your specific presence and perspective? When you encounter someone else's work in critique, what is your first instinct — to assess it, to identify with it, to question it? What would it mean to attend to it before doing any of those things? How does your practice change when it's in dialogue with others? What has a peer's question or response revealed to you about your own work?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — on the studio event as a site of collective thinking, and techniques of relation as a domain of practice.
Research-Creation36   Making Public15   Failure as Method26   Entanglement26Collective PracticeThe methodology holding critical inquiry, technical exploration, and creative production together as co-constitutive practices — not sequential phases, but registers of the same act.Manning & Massumi locate research-creation at the prebifurcation point: the moment before thinking and making diverge into separate institutional structures. At that point, making is already thinking-in-action, and conceptualization is a practice in its own right. The problem research-creation names — and refuses — is the communication model: the assumption that you research first, then make something that delivers the results.The alternative is conditioning over framing. Rather than setting up a question and then answering it, you bring co-causes into interaction and stay open to what emerges. This requires what Manning & Massumi call techniques of relation — structural devices for catalyzing interaction between forces that wouldn't otherwise meet. They are not content-specific; they transfer across disciplines and practices.For this course, the implication is practical: the Critical Technical Journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate — or the work isn't research-creation.
Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 103, Week 114 Where in your workflow do making and thinking happen in the same moment — not sequentially, but simultaneously? Can you locate that moment and work from it deliberately? What would it mean for your project to be conditioned rather than framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If you had to say what your practice is thinking right now — not what you're making, but what the act of making is already processing — what would you say? What institutional structures (program requirements, evaluation criteria, submission formats) separate your thinking from your making? How do you work inside those structures without simply reproducing them?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — the foundational text. Propositions 0–3 define research-creation, enabling constraints, and techniques of relation.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog*3 — on curiosity as a legitimate research methodology; what it means to follow a question rather than test a hypothesis.

item.title: GMAP 395 - SU24 - In-Class Lab - Basic Shader in Unity Shader Graph
item.description: Gain hands-on experience creating and modifying basic shaders using Unity's Shader Graph. Unity 2022.3 Basic understanding of Unity interface Universal Render Pipeline (URP) set up in your project In Unity, right-click in the Project window Select Create > Shader > Universal Render Pipeline > Unlit Shader Graph Name it "MyFirstShaderGraph" Double-click to open it in the Shader Graph window In the Shader Graph window, locate the Blackboard (usually on the left side) In the Blackboard: Click the + button Choose Color from the dropdown Name it _Color (or any appropriate name) Set a default color if desired (found in the Graph Inspector > Node Settings) In the graph area: Click and drag the _Color property from the Blackboard directly into the graph area Connect the Color property node's output to the Base Color input of the "Fragment" node Click "Save Asset" to save your shader graph In Unity, create a new 3D object (e.g., Sphere) in your scene Create a new material: Right-click in the Project window > Create > Material Name it appropriately In the new material's Inspector: Set the Shader to your "Shader Graph/MyFirstShaderGraph" Adjust the Color property to see changes on your 3D object In the Blackboard, add the following properties: Texture2D named _MainTex Vector2 named _Tiling (set default to 1,1) Vector2 named _Offset (set default to 0,0) In your Shader Graph, add the following nodes: Drag the _MainTex, _Tiling, and _Offset properties from the Blackboard into the graph Add a Tiling And Offsetnode Add a Sample Texture 2D node Hotkey SPACEBAR is the hotkey shortcut to open the create node dialogue box. Connect the nodes: Connect the _Tiling and _Offset outputs to the respective inputs of the Tiling And Offset node Connect the UV output of Tiling And Offset to the UV input of Sample Texture 2D Connect the _MainTex property to the Texture input of Sample Texture 2D Add a Multiply node Connect: The RGBA output of Sample Texture 2D to one input of Multiply The _Color property to the other input of Multiply The output of Multiply to the Base Color of the Fragment node Save the Shader Graph Select your 3D object in the scene In the Inspector, you should now see slots for Texture, Tiling, and Offset Assign a texture to the Texture slot Adjust Tiling and Offset values to see how they affect the texture In the Blackboard, add these Float properties: _WaveAmount (default 1) _WaveSpeed (default 1) _WaveFrequency (default 1) In your Shader Graph, add these nodes: Drag the new Float properties from the Blackboard into the graph Add Time node Add Position node (set to World) Add Sine node Add several Multiply (3) nodes Add Add node Add Split node Connect the nodes to create the wave effect: Connect the output of the World Position node to the input of the Split node Connect the R output of the Split node (which represents the X component) to one input of a Multiply node Connect the _WaveFrequency to the other input of this Multiply node Multiply _WaveSpeed by Time Add the results of the above two operations using an Add node Feed the output of the Add node into the Sine node Multiply the Sine output by _WaveAmount Add a Combine node: Connect the R (X) and B (Z) from the Split node to the corresponding inputs on the Combine For the G(Y) input of the Combine node, Add the wave calculation to the G(Y) output of the Split node and connect it to the G(Y) input. Connect the Combine node's output (RGBA or RGB) to the Position input of the Vertex node Save the Shader Graph Select your 3D object in the scene In the Inspector, you should now see Wave Amount, Wave Speed, and Wave Frequency properties Adjust these values to see how they affect the object's shape Modify your shader to blend between two colors based on a custom parameter. In the Blackboard, add: Another Color property named _Color2 A Float property named _BlendFactor (set range 0 to 1) Modes in Graph Inspector You can change the Mode of a property in the Graph Inspector to something like Slider In the graph area: Drag the new properties from the Blackboard Add a Lerp node Connect the nodes: Connect _Color and _Color2 to the A and B inputs of the Lerp node respectively Connect _BlendFactor to the T input of the Lerp node Use the output of the Lerp node in your final color calculation (e.g., multiply it with your texture sample) Save the Shader Graph and adjust the Blend Factor in your material's Inspector to blend between the two colors. Try blending based on vertex position instead of a custom parameter Implement a smooth transition that cycles between the colors over time (Time or Sine) Add a third color and blend between all three Check Remember to save your Shader Graph after each major change, and don't hesitate to experiment with different connections and values!

item.title: GMAP 395 - SU24 - Assignment - Game Art Conceptualization
item.description: In this assignment, you will create a conceptual pitch document for your final game art production project. This project will be an individual effort to create a short, original interactive game art experience that showcases your skills in procedural workflows, custom shaders, visual effects, game audio implementation, and game lighting. Your concept should outline a cohesive vision for a prop, character, or environment-focused experience that will incorporate elements from each module of the course. Choose one of the following focus areas for your project: Prop-focused experience Character-focused experience Environment-focused experience Your concept must incorporate procedural workflows and elements from each course module: Procedural + Modular Modeling and Workflows Material + Shader Development Image + Particle Effects Lighting + Camera Effects Game Audio and Implementation The final project must be (minimally) interactive and showcase your custom-built elements in a meaningful way. While you may use existing assets for supporting elements, all VFX, shaders, and materials must be original creations. Your concept should consider how the interactive element will allow users to experience and appreciate your work in a simulated game setting. A pitch document (PDF format) that includes: Project title and brief tagline Concept overview (100-300 words) Visual target: Include mood boards, style references, or concept sketches Technical breakdown: List the key technical features you plan to implement Interactivity description: Explain how users will interact with your creation Production pipeline: Outline your planned workflow and tools Additional factors that can influence your grade within these ranges include: Creativity and originality of the concept Clarity and professionalism of the pitch document Feasibility of the project within the course timeframe Depth of understanding demonstrated for each technical element Quality and relevance of visual references and mood boards "Lightsaber Forge" is an interactive, prop-focused experience that puts players in the role of a Jedi weaponsmith. Using procedural generation techniques, players will craft unique lightsabers by choosing and manipulating lightsaber components, such as energy crystals, activation switches, and blade guards.With this procedural system each lightsaber creation will reflect the choices and personality of its crafter. Once forged, players can test their lightsaber by igniting the blade and swinging it around, experiencing the weight, balance, and energy signature of their unique weapon.Show, don't tell for this section, images and video links are far better than words here.“GMAP 395 - Mood board Example.png” could not be found.1 Procedural Modeling System: Generate unique lightsaber components Implement a modular assembly system for seamless component integration Custom Shader Development: Create an "energy flow" shader for lightsaber blades with customizable properties Develop a "holographic interface" shader for the forge's control panels Particle and VFX System: Design a dynamic spark and energy particle system for the forging process Implement a blade ignition effect with procedurally generated plasma tendrils Lighting and Camera Effects: Create a reactive lighting system that responds to lightsaber properties Implement a zoom camera effect for focusing on details Procedural Audio Generation: Develop a system for generating unique lightsaber hum and swing sounds based on the saber's properties Create an ambient audio system for the forge environment Players will interact with the forge through a combination of gesture-based controls and UI interfaces. The forging process will be divided into stages: Crystal Selection: Choose and manipulate the core crystal, setting the base properties of the lightsaber. Assembly: Combine components in a 3D space, with real-time feedback on balance and power. Tuning: Fine-tune the lightsaber's energy flow and blade properties using UI controls. Testing: Enter a training arena to test the lightsaber's feel and performance. Concept and Design: Finalize the visual style and user interface layout Procedural Systems Development: Create the core generation systems for components and effects Shader and VFX Creation: Develop custom shaders and particle systems 3D Asset Creation: Design base assets for procedural modification UI Implementation: Develop the holographic interface system (UI + shader) Audio System: Implement procedural audio generation and ambient sound design Integration and Testing: Combine all elements and refine the user experience Polish and Optimization: Fine-tune performance and visual fidelity
